idiom_name: stage list plus driver loop over a shared stage contract
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: fix one stage contract (usually value -> value, plus an agreed failure and cancellation channel), name each transformation as a separate function or object, keep them in an ordered list, and let a single driver execute the list, forwarding each result and applying the error, cancellation and instrumentation policy in one place. Prefer streaming stages that pass one item through at a time when the payload is a sequence, and a linear driver over a single value otherwise. The classic Pipeline class (add stage, execute) is one encoding of this; where the language already names the concept - stream pipelines, sequence operators, channel stages, publisher chains - use that realization instead and keep only the language-neutral description for cross-language documentation. Key realizations include: (1) eager sequence: stages run immediately in a for-loop or fold; (2) lazy chain: stages are composed via function composition and a terminal operation triggers execution (collection pipeline); (3) streaming: stages are connected by bounded queues or channels and run concurrently (async generator, Reactor Flux, Rx Observable); (4) dataflow DAG: a directed acyclic graph where each node is a stage and edges are data dependencies, used by workflow orchestrators (Airflow, Kubeflow, Prefect, Dagster).
code_sketch:
stages = [parse, validate, enrich]        # named, ordered, one responsibility each
value  = source()
for stage in stages:                      # the driver owns order and error policy
    value = stage(value)
sink(value)
pitfalls: Mixing value transformers and side-effecting handlers in one list without a contract makes ordering, failure and retry behaviour unpredictable.
The driver is the only place that can enforce error, cancellation and instrumentation policy; letting each call site run its own loop makes pipelines diverge.
Lazy realizations do nothing until the terminal operation runs, so a pipeline that is assembled and never consumed fails silently.

Wrong move: treat a pipeline as a durable workflow -> an in-memory stage driver cannot resume after process loss or model human or conditional transitions -> instead use a workflow orchestrator when execution must persist, branch or wait for external events.

Wrong move: put an unbounded queue between stages -> a slow consumer turns backlog into memory exhaustion and hides demand -> instead bound the buffer and propagate backpressure or apply an explicit drop or spill policy.
Wrong move: make side-effecting stages blindly retryable -> retries can duplicate writes or messages -> instead make effects idempotent or isolate commit and compensation policy in the driver.
